parsedVerdict.reasoning: CancelOrderUseCase does what an application use case should: it coordinates the work and leaves the decisions to the domain. It loads the order from the repository and asks the domain function canCancelOrder whether the order can be cancelled. It then tells the Catalog to release each item's stock and saves the order. Nothing in the file comes from a web or transport package: no request or response types, no HTTP status codes and no HTTP errors. The method execute(orderId: string): Order uses only plain values and types the project declares itself. The only thing it throws is the standard JavaScript Error. The constructor takes a Catalog and an OrderRepository, which is dependency wiring and allowed by the rubric. The file has no framework decorators or base classes, no ORM code, and no direct database, file or HTTP access. A side note that doesn't affect this rule: execute never changes the order's state to cancelled before saving it. That looks like a logic bug, not a layer violation.
